items.stem: Define the term 'vicarious liability'.
items.answer: Liability imposed on one person (usually an employer) for the torts of another (usually an employee) committed in the course of employment, although the employer is not personally at fault.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. liability imposed on one person (usually an employer) for the torts of another (usually an employee) committed in the course of employment, although the employer is not personally at fault. [2]

items.stem: Nadia works for Elena Ltd as a delivery driver in Karachi. On a day off, Nadia borrowed the company van to help a friend move house and hit Mateo, a pedestrian. Identify the main legal issue raised and state the relevant legal rule.
items.answer: Vicarious liability. Stage 1: employee or relationship akin to employment (Ready Mixed Concrete; Catholic Child Welfare Society; Barclays 2020).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies vicarious liability. 1 mark: states the rule correctly, e.g. stage 1: employee or relationship akin to employment (Ready Mixed Concrete; Catholic Child Welfare Society; Barclays 2020). [2]

items.stem: Amara works for Jonas Ltd as a kiosk attendant at a petrol station in Dhaka. After an argument with a customer, Mei, about service at the counter, Amara followed Mei outside and punched Mei. Advise Mei whether Jonas Ltd is vicariously liable. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: stage 1: employee or relationship akin to employment (Ready Mixed Concrete; Catholic Child Welfare Society; Barclays 2020); stage 2: tort closely connected with employment (Lister v Hesley Hall; Mohamud v Morrison); prohibited acts in the course of the job (Limpus; Rose v Plenty) v acts outside it (Twine; Hilton - frolic). Application: Amara is an employee of Jonas Ltd; the tort was an unbroken sequence connected with the job, so the close connection test is likely satisfied (Mohamud). Conclusion: Jonas Ltd is liable only if the tort was in the course of employment: here it was an unbroken sequence connected with the job, so the close connection test is likely satisfied (Mohamud).

items.stem: Mohammed accepted a lift from Mateo after a party in Istanbul, knowing that Mateo was very drunk. Mohammed did not wear a seat belt, which would have prevented the injuries altogether. Mateo crashed and Mohammed was injured. Identify the main legal issue raised and state the relevant legal rule.
items.answer: Defences of volenti and contributory negligence. Volenti requires full knowledge and free acceptance of the risk (Smith v Baker; Morris v Murray), but s149 Road Traffic Act 1988 excludes it for passengers.

items.stem: Ana accepted a lift from Tomás after a party in Santiago, knowing that Tomás was very drunk. Ana wore a seat belt. Tomás crashed and Ana was injured. Advise Tomás on the defences available against Ana's claim. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: volenti requires full knowledge and free acceptance of the risk (Smith v Baker; Morris v Murray), but s149 Road Traffic Act 1988 excludes it for passengers; contributory negligence reduces damages under the 1945 Act; accepting a lift from a drunk driver (Owens v Brimmell) and not wearing a seat belt (Froom v Butcher); illegality may apply to joint criminal enterprises (Pitts v Hunt). Application: volenti cannot apply because of s149 Road Traffic Act 1988; Ana knew Tomás was very drunk, so damages may be reduced (Owens v Brimmell); seat belt: no seat belt reduction. Conclusion: Tomás cannot rely on volenti, but Ana's damages will be reduced for contributory negligence, including no seat belt reduction.

items.stem: Explain how contributory negligence operates.
items.answer: Under the Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 s1, where the claimant's own fault contributed to the damage, the court reduces damages by such amount as is just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share of responsibility (e.g. Froom v Butcher: 15%-25% for seat belts).

items.stem: Ravi, a teacher aged 55, was seriously injured in an accident caused by Sipho's negligence. Ravi can no longer work and needs daily care. Explain the types of damages that Ravi could claim. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: damages aim to put the claimant in the position as if the tort had not occurred; special damages: past lost earnings and expenses; general damages: pain, suffering and loss of amenity (H West v Shephard; Heil v Rankin) and future loss of earnings and care; lump sum or periodical payments (Damages Act 1996); provisional damages where deterioration is possible. Application: Ravi can no longer work and needs daily care; past losses are special damages; pain, suffering and loss of amenity and future losses are general damages; periodical payments may suit long-term care needs. Conclusion: Ravi can claim special damages for past losses and general damages for non-pecuniary and future losses.

items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. liability imposed on one person (usually an employer) for the torts of another (usually an employee) committed in the course of employment, although the employer is not personally at fault. [2]

items.stem: Explain the policy reasons for imposing vicarious liability.
items.answer: The employer is more likely to have the means to compensate and insurance; it benefits from the employee's work and should bear the risks; it encourages employers to supervise and train staff and to choose them carefully.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per reason, up to 3. [3]

items.stem: Mei works for Noah Ltd as a kiosk attendant at a petrol station in Madrid. After an argument with a customer, Elena, about service at the counter, Mei followed Elena outside and punched Elena. State, with a brief reason, the most likely legal outcome.
items.answer: Noah Ltd is liable only if the tort was in the course of employment: here it was an unbroken sequence connected with the job, so the close connection test is likely satisfied (Mohamud). Reason: stage 1: employee or relationship akin to employment (Ready Mixed Concrete; Catholic Child Welfare Society; Barclays 2020)

items.stem: Mateo works for Felix Ltd as a kiosk attendant at a petrol station in Lima. After an argument with a customer, Arjun, about service at the counter, Mateo followed Arjun outside and punched Arjun. Advise Arjun whether Felix Ltd is vicariously liable. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: stage 1: employee or relationship akin to employment (Ready Mixed Concrete; Catholic Child Welfare Society; Barclays 2020); stage 2: tort closely connected with employment (Lister v Hesley Hall; Mohamud v Morrison); prohibited acts in the course of the job (Limpus; Rose v Plenty) v acts outside it (Twine; Hilton - frolic). Application: Mateo is an employee of Felix Ltd; the tort was an unbroken sequence connected with the job, so the close connection test is likely satisfied (Mohamud). Conclusion: Felix Ltd is liable only if the tort was in the course of employment: here it was an unbroken sequence connected with the job, so the close connection test is likely satisfied (Mohamud).

items.stem: Evaluate the development of vicarious liability in recent years.
items.answer: For: close connection test gives justice to abuse victims (Lister); relationships akin to employment cover modern working patterns; Barclays (2020) and Morrison (2020) set sensible limits. Against: uncertainty about what is "fair and just"; burden on charities and small employers; gig economy relationships remain unclear. Conclusion: The law has expanded to meet social needs but now has clearer limits.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge and understanding [5]: accurate explanation of the law with supporting authority, e.g. Lister v Hesley Hall (2001); Catholic Child Welfare Society (2012); Mohamud v Morrison (2016); Barclays v Various Claimants (2020); WM Morrison v Various Claimants (2020). AO3 Analysis and evaluation [7]: arguments supporting the view, e.g. close connection test gives justice to abuse victims (Lister); relationships akin to employment cover modern working patterns; Barclays (2020) and Morrison (2020) set sensible limits; arguments against / problems, e.g. uncertainty about what is "fair and just"; burden on charities and small employers; gig economy relationships remain unclear. items.stem: State what is meant by 'volenti non fit injuria'.
items.answer: A complete defence where the claimant, with full knowledge of the nature and extent of the risk, freely and voluntarily agreed to accept it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. a complete defence where the claimant, with full knowledge of the nature and extent of the risk, freely and voluntarily agreed to accept it. [2]

items.stem: Briefly explain the legal principle established in Dann v Hamilton (1939).
items.answer: Facts: a passenger accepted a lift from a driver who had been drinking and was injured in a crash. Principle: Volenti failed because the driver was not so drunk that the passenger must have accepted the risk.

items.stem: Using Smith v Baker & Sons (1891) as an example, explain how the courts approach defences in tort.
items.answer: Facts: a quarry worker knew stones were swung over his head by a crane, and one fell on him. Principle: Mere knowledge of a risk does not mean the claimant consented to it. This shows how the law on defences in tort is applied.

items.stem: State what is meant by 'compensatory damages'.
items.answer: Damages that aim to put the claimant, so far as money can, in the position they would have been in if the tort had not been committed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. damages that aim to put the claimant, so far as money can, in the position they would have been in if the tort had not been committed. [2]

items.stem: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of lump-sum damages.
items.answer: Advantages: finality, the claimant can control the money; disadvantages: it is based on predictions about the future that may be wrong, may be spent too quickly or run out; periodical payments (Damages Act 1996) and provisional damages address this.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark disadvantage; 1 mark alternative. [3]

items.answer: Special $24,000; general $40,000; total $64,000.

items.stem: Explain the main limitation periods in tort.
items.answer: Personal injury: 3 years from injury or date of knowledge (s11, s14), with a discretion to extend (s33); other torts: 6 years from damage (s2); latent damage in negligence (not personal injury): 6 years or 3 years from knowledge, with a 15-year longstop (s14A, s14B); time does not run against a child until 18 (s28).
items.markingKey: 1 mark personal injury; 1 mark general 6 years; 1 mark latent damage/longstop or minors. [3]

items.stem: Briefly explain the legal principle established in A v Hoare (2008).
items.answer: Facts: a woman sued a man who had attacked her years earlier after he won a large lottery prize. Principle: The court can use its s33 discretion to extend the limitation period for claims for deliberate assaults.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant facts (a woman sued a man who had attacked her years earlier after he won a large lottery prize). 1 mark: the principle/decision (the court can use its s33 discretion to extend the limitation period for claims for deliberate assaults). [2]

items.stem: Explain two criticisms of the fault-based system of compensation in tort.
items.answer: It is costly and slow, with high legal costs; outcomes depend on proving fault, so similar injuries are treated differently; it may encourage a compensation culture and defensive practices; a no-fault scheme (New Zealand) may be fairer.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark criticism, 1 mark development). [4]

items.stem: Freya was injured on 10 October 2018 when a faulty machine at work injured Freya's back. Freya knew immediately that the injury was serious and who caused it. Freya wants to sue now, four years later. Identify the main legal issue raised and state the relevant legal rule.
items.answer: Limitation periods under the Limitation Act 1980. Personal injury: three years from injury or date of knowledge (s11, s14 Limitation Act 1980).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies limitation periods under the Limitation Act 1980. 1 mark: states the rule correctly, e.g. personal injury: three years from injury or date of knowledge (s11, s14 Limitation Act 1980). [2]
